group.title: Mind and behaviour
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Connected with thinking, learning and remembering.
examples: Puzzles may help keep your {cognitive} skills sharp.
wrong: Running is a purely cognitive activity that uses no muscles.

words.meaning: The way you notice and understand something through the senses or mind.
examples: Tiredness can change your {perception} of time.
wrong: Perception is the part of the body that digests food.

words.meaning: A sudden strong wish to do something without thinking.
examples: I bought the coat on {impulse}.
wrong: She acted on impulse after months of careful planning.

words.meaning: Hard to stop or control, done again and again.
examples: He is a {compulsive} liar.
wrong: Her compulsive checking happened only once a year.

words.meaning: A quiet person who gets energy from time alone.
examples: As an {introvert}, she needs time alone after parties.
wrong: The introvert loves being the center of attention at every party.

words.meaning: A lively person who gets energy from being with others.
examples: An {extrovert} like Tom loves meeting new people.
wrong: The extrovert avoids people and stays home alone.

words.meaning: Existing in the mind without you being aware of it.
examples: Dreams may reveal {subconscious} fears.
wrong: His subconscious plan was one he thought about clearly every day.

words.meaning: A natural way of acting or feeling that is not learned.
examples: Birds build nests by {instinct}.
wrong: Babies learn their instincts from books at school.

words.meaning: The ability to know something by feeling rather than reasoning.
examples: My {intuition} told me something was wrong.
wrong: She used intuition, carefully checking every fact step by step.

words.meaning: How much you value and respect yourself.
examples: Praise can boost a child’s {self-esteem}.
wrong: With high self-esteem, he thought he was worthless.

words.meaning: Training that makes a person or animal react in a set way.
examples: Through {conditioning}, the dog learned to sit at the sound of a bell.
wrong: Conditioning means behavior that is never shaped by experience.

words.meaning: Rewards or responses that make a behavior more likely to happen again.
examples: Positive {reinforcement} works better than punishment.
wrong: Positive reinforcement means scolding a child for good work.

words.meaning: Refusing to accept that something unpleasant is true.
examples: He’s in {denial} about how much he drinks.
wrong: She was in denial, so she openly admitted the problem.

words.meaning: The influence that people your own age have on what you do.
examples: Teens often start smoking because of {peer pressure}.
wrong: Peer pressure comes only from your grandparents.

words.meaning: Behaving in the same way as most people in a group.
examples: School uniforms encourage {conformity}.
wrong: His conformity made him dress very differently from everyone.

words.meaning: A person’s basic nature, especially how they react emotionally.
examples: She has a calm {temperament} and rarely gets angry.
wrong: Temperament is the temperature of a room.

words.meaning: A person’s usual mood or attitude.
examples: He has a cheerful {disposition}.
wrong: Her sunny disposition made her gloomy and bad-tempered.

words.meaning: A particular quality in someone’s character.
examples: Honesty is her best {trait}.
wrong: A trait is a type of fruit grown in hot countries.

words.meaning: A fixed way of thinking about things.
examples: A growth {mindset} helps you learn from mistakes.
wrong: A mindset is a set of tools for fixing a bike.

words.meaning: The strength of mind to control what you do.
examples: It takes {willpower} to stick to a diet.
wrong: He showed great willpower by giving in to every temptation.

words.meaning: Choosing to wait for a bigger reward rather than taking a small one now.
examples: Saving money for years is a form of {delayed gratification}.
wrong: Spending all your pay at once is a good example of delayed gratification.

words.meaning: The discomfort of holding two beliefs or acts that do not match.
examples: Smokers who know the risks often feel {cognitive dissonance}.
wrong: Cognitive dissonance is the calm you feel when your actions match your beliefs.

words.meaning: Believing something because you want it to be true, not because it is.
examples: Expecting to pass without studying is {wishful thinking}.
wrong: Wishful thinking is a careful look at hard facts.

words.meaning: To think deeply and for a long time, often in a worrying way.
examples: She kept {ruminating} on what she should have said.
wrong: He ruminated on the problem without giving it a thought.

words.meaning: Careful thought about your own feelings and reasons.
examples: The retreat was a time for quiet {introspection}.
wrong: Introspection means studying other people, never yourself.

words.meaning: A very strong and unreasonable fear of something.
examples: He has a {phobia} of spiders.
wrong: Her phobia of heights makes her love climbing cliffs.

words.meaning: A way of dealing with stress or difficult feelings.
examples: Running is my main {coping mechanism} when work gets hard.
wrong: A coping mechanism is something that makes stress much worse on purpose.

words.meaning: A strong dislike of something.
examples: Cats have an {aversion} to water.
wrong: His aversion to chocolate means he eats it every day.

words.meaning: A natural feeling that makes you want to act in a certain way.
examples: My first {inclination} was to say no.
wrong: She had no inclination to rest, so she lay down at once.

words.meaning: A thought or interest that fills your mind all the time.
examples: His {obsession} with his phone worries his parents.
wrong: An obsession is something you hardly ever think about.

words.meaning: Caring about others and helping them without wanting anything back.
examples: Giving a kidney to a stranger is pure {altruism}.
wrong: His altruism showed when he kept every cent for himself.

words.meaning: Cleverly controlling others for your own benefit, often unfairly.
examples: A {manipulative} boss uses guilt to make staff work late.
wrong: Her manipulative nature made her always honest and open with people.

words.meaning: Clear knowledge of your own character, feelings and actions.
examples: Good leaders have strong {self-awareness}.
wrong: With self-awareness, he had no idea how he came across.

words.meaning: The habit of noticing only facts that support what you already believe.
examples: {Confirmation bias} makes people read only news they agree with.
wrong: Confirmation bias makes people search hard for facts against their own views.

words.meaning: Not based on clear thinking or reason.
examples: I know it’s {irrational}, but I hate flying.
wrong: His irrational choice was based on careful logic.

words.meaning: How long a person can stay focused on something.
examples: Young children have a short {attention span}.
wrong: A long attention span means you get bored after a few seconds.

words.meaning: To push painful feelings or memories out of your mind.
examples: He {repressed} his anger and smiled.
wrong: She repressed her feelings by shouting them out to everyone.

words.meaning: Likely to behave or think in a certain way, or to get an illness.
examples: Some people are {predisposed} to anxiety.
wrong: He is predisposed to trust people, so he suspects everyone.

words.meaning: Done often and regularly, as a habit.
examples: He is a {habitual} late riser.
wrong: Her habitual walk happened once in her whole life.

words.meaning: The mood or attitude you are in at a particular time.
examples: Wait until he’s in a better {frame of mind} before you ask.
wrong: A frame of mind is something you hang a picture in.
